sections.label: Singapore net-zero emissions ambition
sections.summary: Singapore will raise its ambition to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 and revise its Nationally Determined Contribution to peak emissions earlier and reduce to around 60 million tonnes by 2030.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Two weeks ago, at the Singapore International Energy Week, Deputy Prime Minister Wong announced that Singapore will raise our ambition to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: We will also revise our medium-term international commitment – our Nationally Determined Contribution, or NDC – to peak our emissions earlier, and reduce our emissions to around 60 million tonnes by 2030.

sections.label: Carbon tax levels and transition framework
sections.summary: The Bill amends the Carbon Pricing Act to adopt carbon tax levels of $25 per tonne in 2024 and 2025 and $45 per tonne in 2026 and beyond, and inserts sections 20A to 20G for an industry transition framework.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: First, the Bill will amend the Third Schedule to the Carbon Pricing Act, or CPA, to adopt the revised carbon tax levels of $25 per tonne for greenhouse gas emissions in 2024 and 2025, and $45 per tonne for greenhouse gas emissions in 2026 and beyond.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: The progressive increases will set us on a trajectory to reach between $50 to $80 per tonne by 2030.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Second, the Bill will insert new sections 20A to 20G in Part 5 of the CPA to set out the broad parameters of the industry transition framework, which will provide transitory allowances to companies in Emissions-Intensive Trade-Exposed, or EITE, sectors that face intense competition in the global market.

sections.label: International Carbon Credits framework
sections.summary: The Bill sets up the International Carbon Credits framework through sections 33A to 33D in Part 5 of the Carbon Pricing Act.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Third, the Bill will set up the International Carbon Credits framework, or ICC framework, through sections 33A to 33D in Part 5 of the CPA.

sections.label: Companies using eligible carbon credits
sections.summary: Under the ICC framework, companies will have the option to tap on eligible ICC to fulfil part of their carbon tax liability.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Under the ICC framework, companies will have the option to tap on eligible ICC to fulfil part of their carbon tax liability.

sections.label: ICC definition and carbon tax payment
sections.summary: The Bill introduces the definition of an ICC as a certificate representing one tonne of emissions reductions or removals from projects outside Singapore, and allows companies to surrender eligible ICC as a valid alternative mode of carbon tax payment.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: First, to introduce the definition of an ICC, as a certificate representing one tonne of emissions reductions or removals generated from projects and programmes outside Singapore; and two, to allow companies to surrender eligible ICC as a valid alternative mode of carbon tax payment, in addition to FPCC.

sections.label: ICC cap and domestic abatement priority
sections.summary: Domestic abatement remains the priority, and new section 33B stipulates that ICC surrendered must be capped at a prescribed facility-level limit, currently intended at 5% of taxable emissions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: I should emphasise that while the ICC framework provides a complementary pathway for companies to decarbonise, reducing emissions through domestic abatement efforts will remain our priority.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: Hence, the new section 33B will stipulate that the ICC surrendered must be capped at a prescribed facility-level limit.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: This is currently intended to be set at 5% of taxable emissions and will be prescribed in the subsidiary legislation.

sections.label: Removing nitrogen trifluoride from Second Schedule
sections.summary: The Bill amends the Second Schedule to remove nitrogen trifluoride as a non-reckonable greenhouse gas, bringing its emissions under the carbon tax from 2024.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: The Bill will also amend the Second Schedule to remove nitrogen trifluoride (NF3), as a non-reckonable greenhouse gas.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: This will bring NF3 emissions within the coverage of the carbon tax.

sentences.speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
sentences.text: We intend to do so from 2024 onwards.

sections.label: Government net-zero 2050 announcement
sections.summary: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong announced last month that Singapore will aim to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Since then, the Government has responded clearly and positively.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: There was Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's announcement last month that Singapore will aim to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050.

sections.label: No end date for allowances
sections.summary: The passage asks why the Bill sets no end date for granting allowances meant to reduce near-term impact on business competitiveness.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Second, given that the allowances are meant to reduce the "near-term impact" on business competitiveness, why does the Bill set no end date for such allowances to be granted?

sections.label: Carbon and fuel tax coverage
sections.summary: The carbon tax and transport fuel tax currently cover 90% of the nation's emissions.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: Our carbon tax, along with our transport fuel tax, currently covers 90% of our nation's emissions.

sections.label: Publishing international carbon credit data
sections.summary: The passage asks whether the Ministry will consider publishing data on trends in international carbon credits used by companies and facilities.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: In addition, given that companies may now buy international carbon credits instead of paying carbon tax for up to 5% of taxable emissions, will the Ministry also consider publishing data on trends in ICCs used by companies and facilities?

sections.label: Guterres warning and optimism
sections.summary: The passage cites UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres on growing emissions and irreversible climate chaos, but the speaker remains optimistic about progress.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: The sadness and, perhaps worry, is fuelled by what UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said just yesterday: "Greenhouse gas emissions keep growing.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: And our planet is fast approaching tipping points that will make climate chaos irreversible.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: We are on a highway to climate hell with our foot on the accelerator." But – and it is a big "but" – I remain optimistic, and I hope we all do.

sentences.speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
sentences.text: There is so much progress made, so much more people joining this movement and millions wanting to take action.

sections.label: Workers' Party carbon tax amendments
sections.summary: The Workers' Party supports the Bill but proposes amendments to limit carbon tax allowances and increase transparency and accountability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: While we support the thrust of this Bill, the Workers' Party has some amendments to suggest.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Our amendments, while accepting the principle that the Government can and should create allowances to reduce the carbon tax paid in specific cases, seek to limit the scope and extent of allowances; and to increase transparency and accountability, so as to ensure that the carbon pricing regime is seen to be fair, clear and uniformly applicable to all, which enhances public buy-in, while at the same time, making sure that it is a sufficiently robust nudge to businesses to find the best ways to reduce emissions.

sections.label: Amendments filed by MPs
sections.summary: The Workers' Party's proposed amendments were filed by Ms He Ting Ru and the speaker.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The Workers' Party's proposed amendments to this Bill have been filed by my Parliamentary colleague, Sengkang Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru, and myself.

sections.label: Survey on climate targets
sections.summary: Of 490 responses, 94% of respondents were willing to withstand trade-offs and inconveniences to achieve enhanced climate targets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Of the 490 responses, 94% of respondents were willing to withstand trade-offs and inconveniences to achieve enhanced climate targets.

sections.label: Limiting carbon tax allowances
sections.summary: Carbon tax allowances mean all large emitters pay the tax but some pay less, and there is a case to limit them in extent and time.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Carbon tax allowances, on the other hand, mean that all large emitters have to pay the carbon tax, but some large emitters have to pay less when awarded an allowance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: There is a strong case to circumscribe the carbon tax allowances awarded in terms of extent as well as in terms of time.

sections.label: Amendments to Minister's allowance powers
sections.summary: Amendments were tabled to limit the Minister's powers to award non-time-limited allowances, and the President's recommendation is needed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Only then will we obtain a wider buy-in to the carbon tax regime from citizens and the business community that we need.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Hence, we have tabled amendments to the broad powers given to the Minister to pick and choose taxable facilities to award non-time-limited allowances to.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Creating a more limited allowance regime sends a stronger signal about how we intend to approach the carbon tax and ensures that no government of the day can prop up any large emitter in perpetuity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
sentences.text: At this point, Mr Speaker, Sir, perhaps I should add that before these amendments, both mine and Ms He Ting Ru's, can be voted on at the Committee stage later, I understand that we need the President's recommendation as these are tax-related and have fiscal implications.

sections.label: Cap of 33% allowance
sections.summary: The amendment sets a cap of 33% because the tax charged must not be less than double the awarded allowance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: In other words, our amendment sets up a cap of 33%, because the tax charged must not be less than double the awarded allowance.

sections.label: Public registry allowance disclosure
sections.summary: The proposed public registry would include the registered person receiving allowances and the Minister's reasons for awarding them, which the current Bill does not require.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The information which is required to be included in this public registry that we are proposing, in addition to that referring to the number of emissions years the allowance is applicable to and the methodology for calculating this, include: "(c) the registered person of the taxable facility who has received allowances; and (d) the Minister's reasons for deciding to award the allowances.".

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: The current version of the Bill does not require the Minister to disclose allowances or any details on them.

sections.label: Definition of carbon tax allowance
sections.summary: A carbon tax allowance is a tax reduction applied to one entity, unlike all similar entities that pay the tax.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: A carbon tax allowance is a reduction in tax applied to one entity, versus all similar entities which have to pay that tax.

sections.label: Registry omits award quantity
sections.summary: The proposal does not require disclosing the quantity of the award, and a deletion aims to reduce executive discretion and balance discretion with a transparent rules-based system.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: To address the competitive concerns and the concerns about Government agencies having a legitimate interest in not revealing the amount of the award or the terms of the award given to specific companies in specific cases, our proposal for a public registry does not require information about the quantity of the award to be disclosed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: I repeat – it does not require information about the quantity of the award to be disclosed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: We propose this deletion so as to eliminate a provision that might allow a Minister to disregard the formula specified in the previous section for the maximum cap for an allowance.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: In short, we believe that deleting those lines reduces overly broad executive discretion and strikes a better balance point – between legitimate executive discretion on the one hand and creating a transparent, rules-based system on the other hand.

sections.label: Amendments strengthen Bill's thrust
sections.summary: The proposed amendments are said to strengthen the Bill, enhance public acceptance, and better align it with sought climate change outcomes, while avoiding the tragedy of the commons.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: We must avoid the tragedy of the commons – as a country and as a species.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: However, we have proposed a number of amendments that we feel strengthen the thrust of the Bill, make it better and which will enhance wide public acceptance, as well as better align the provisions and effects of the Bill with the climate change outcomes that we seek.

sections.label: EITE sector competitiveness questions
sections.summary: Questions ask how Government will help EITE sectors like electronics, chemical and energy industries stay competitive, prevent job losses, and get large emitters to lead in going green.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: In view of this, how will the Government help EITE sectors, such as the electronics, chemical and energy industries to remain economically competitive?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: How will the Ministry ensure that jobs are not lost to jurisdictions with less stringent legislation?

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: How will the Government get the largest carbon emitters, such as all the energy producers in the world, to take the lead in becoming more green?

sections.label: Carbon tax revenue and price
sections.summary: Questions ask how tax revenue will support residents and decarbonisation, while proposed amendments to the CPA 2018 provide for carbon price and tax rate increases of $50 to $80 per tonne by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
sentences.text: How would the Government use the tax revenue to support our residents and the decarbonisation efforts?

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While the Government has declined to come as far as we have advocated, the proposed amendments to the CPA of 2018 provides for increases to the carbon price and carbon tax rate, which the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) has indicated, will now be in the order of between $50 and $80 per tonne by 2030.

sections.label: Carbon tax rate increase schedule
sections.summary: The Schedule proposes raising the carbon tax from $5 per metric ton until 2023 to $25 in 2024 and 2025, and $45 from 2026 onward.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The Schedule currently proposes an increase of the carbon tax, from $5 per metric ton of carbon dioxide emissions up till 2023, to $25 in 2024 and 2025, and to $45 from 2026 onward.

sections.label: Carbon tax rate flexibility
sections.summary: The $25 rate could drop to $15 or $20 in a recession, or rise to $30 or $35 as the economy rebounds.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For example, if we find ourselves sliding into a recession next year, the $25 rate could drop to $15 or $20, depending on the severity of the contraction, whereas it could rise to $30 or $35 as the economy rebounds.

sections.label: European carbon tax macroeconomic study
sections.summary: A study of a European carbon tax finds no evidence that such taxes are job or growth killers.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: A study that examines the macroeconomic implications of a carbon tax in Europe finds that there is no evidence to support the view that such taxes are job or growth killers.

sections.label: Green Singapore Government Securities launch
sections.summary: MAS oversaw the inaugural launch of $2.4 billion worth of Green Singapore Government Securities in August this year.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The MAS oversaw the inaugural launch of $2.4 billion worth of Green Singapore Government Securities (Green SGS) in August this year.

sections.label: Establishing an EXIM Bank
sections.summary: The Government can support the green transition via financial development by establishing an Export Import Bank.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Another way that the Government can support the green transition via financial development is to establish an Export Import (EXIM) Bank.

sections.label: EXIM bank funding green projects
sections.summary: Green projects, especially in infrastructure, satisfy both criteria, making an EXIM bank ideally positioned to fund them.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Green projects, especially in infrastructure, satisfy both criteria, making an EXIM bank ideally positioned to fund them.

sections.label: EXIM banks green on-lending
sections.summary: The passage states EXIM banks' trade financing and international financial access portfolios could be expanded to include sustainability objectives, and other EXIM banks have rolled out green on-lending facilities.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Consequently, the trade financing and international financial access portfolios of an EXIM bank could easily be expanded to enfold sustainability objectives.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
sentences.text: And indeed, the number of other EXIM banks, such as those in China, India, Hungary and Thailand, have successfully rolled out green on-lending facilities.

sections.label: Carbon pricing and net zero
sections.summary: The speaker supports carbon pricing to peak emissions by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050, while maintaining flexibility for the pathway and final energy supply model.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: That is the whole point of why I am interested in speaking about the mechanism for getting to that process, while we are talking about the carbon tax.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I support the use of carbon pricing as a tool to help us peak carbon emission by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: When Singapore says it is going to do something, it will.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: However, for the transition to net zero, we should maintain some flexibility and adaptability for the pathway to get there and for the final energy supply model.

sections.label: Green hydrogen as energy vector
sections.summary: The passage states that one day, green hydrogen could replace oil and natural gas as the primary energy vector.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: One day, green hydrogen could replace oil and natural gas as the primary energy vector.

sections.label: Energy security and IPCC warning
sections.summary: The speaker asks how the energy supply model will remain secured, resilient and reliable, and cites the UN IPCC warning on limiting global warming.

sentences.speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: We must also be prepared for the proverbial "Perfect Storm".

sentences.speaker: Mr Cheng Hsing Yao (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Thus, I would appreciate if the Minister could outline, as we seek to cut our carbon emissions, how our energy supply model will always be secured, resilient and reliable.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In April this year, the UN IPCC sounded a warning that we are running out of time to make changes to limit global warming.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: It concluded that limiting warming to around 1.5 degrees requires global GHG emissions to peak before 2025 – meaning in the next three years – and to drop by 43% by 2030.

sections.label: Surrendering international carbon credits
sections.summary: The Bill allows facilities to surrender ICCs for up to 5% of taxable emissions, with Clause 33B allowing the Minister to permit excess surrender.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Currently, the Bill allows for facilities to surrender ICCs for up to 5% of their taxable emissions.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Clause 33B of the Bill provides an exception where the Minister may "permit eligible international carbon credits to be surrendered in excess of the prescribed limit in any particular case or class of cases." This means that the percentage could be increased to more than 5% if the Minister permits.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Allowing facilities to use ICCs for a sizeable portion of their emissions may mean that facilities end up having less incentive to cut down on taxable emissions, as they do not have to pay tax on that portion of emissions.

sections.label: Carbon credits quality and eligibility
sections.summary: The speaker seeks clarification on the quality and eligibility of carbon credits, noting NEA signed MOUs with Verra and Gold Standard.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: In addition, I would like to seek clarification on the quality and eligibility of carbon credits.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I understand that NEA has signed separate MOUs with Verra and Gold Standard to support Singapore-based companies in using eligible carbon credits issued by Verra and Gold Standard to meet part of their carbon tax obligations in Singapore.

sections.label: UN offset programme studies
sections.summary: Studies of the CDM and JI found 60% to 70% of their offset credits may not represent valid emissions reductions.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Studies conducted on two of the world's largest offset programmes, which are both administered by the United Nations under the Kyoto Protocol – the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) and Joint implementation (JI) – have found approximately 60% to 70% of their offset credits may not represent valid emissions reductions.

sections.label: Green finance schemes and growth
sections.summary: The GSLS and Project Greenprint aim to grow green finance, with green bonds and green loans increasing.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Initiatives, such as the Green and Sustainability-Linked Loan Grant Scheme (GSLS) and Project Greenprint aim to do just that, and we have also seen that the local green bond market has grown from S$1 billion five years ago to S$14.4 billion last year.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The amount of green loans to has grown from S$2.9 billion in 2018 to S$17 billion last year.

sections.label: Sustainability-linked bond greenwashing risks
sections.summary: Sustainability-linked bond funds are not ring-fenced, and interest penalties are paltry relative to issuer revenue.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: For sustainability-linked bonds, in particular, the funds are not ring-fenced, making them vulnerable to greenwashing and allows financing to continue to be used by issuers to fund carbon-intensive expenses and projects.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: More generally, penalties by way of bumps of less than 100 basis points in the amount of increased interest payable is paltry, especially if these are percentages agreed to by the companies themselves, and often represent amounts that are tiny fractions, that work out to be far under 1% of the annual revenue of these issuers.

sections.label: ICCs threshold and public register
sections.summary: Singapore committed to a 5% ICC threshold and high-quality ICCs, and a public register for threshold waivers is proposed.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Coming back to ICCs, many of the principles of what I have just outlined also apply.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I believe the above points are the reasons why Singapore has committed to the 5% threshold, and it is also important to note our commitment to "high-quality" ICCs.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But given the risks outlined above, I believe we can and should put information out in the public domain, where possible, including the public register for waivers of the threshold for ICCs, which would send a clear signal to emitters that buying their way towards net zero is not an option.

sections.label: Net-zero 2050 stakeholder collaboration
sections.summary: Given Singapore's 2050 net-zero commitment, the question asks how Government will work with stakeholders on decarbonisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Given that Singapore has committed to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 and many large organisations, like the United Overseas Bank which had committed to net zero last week, how does the Government plan to work with the whole ecosystem of stakeholders to help ensure social and economic progress in tandem with decarbonisation to align with Singapore's net-zero emissions policy?

sections.label: Singapore carbon tax in Asia
sections.summary: Within a few years Singapore's carbon tax will be the highest in Asia, placing it among regional decarbonisation leaders.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Within a few years, our carbon tax will be the highest in Asia, placing us amongst leaders in this region for decarbonisation efforts.

sections.label: Cap on large emitters
sections.summary: Asks whether the Government would consider capping greenhouse gases emitted by large emitters such as oil and gas industries.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: In addition to the carbon taxes, would the Government consider putting a cap on the amount of GHGs emitted by large emitters, such as the oil and gas industries?

sections.label: Carbon tax impact on stakeholders
sections.summary: Notes carbon tax impact on SMEs and lower-income individuals, and welcomes revenue-neutral carbon taxes earmarked for decarbonisation.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: (In Mandarin):   While establishing a just transition, we must also remember that there will be an impact of carbon tax on other stakeholders not earmarked as high emitters, including SMEs and lower-income individuals.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: I am heartened that the carbon taxes will be revenue neutral and earmarked to support decarbonisation efforts.

sections.label: Funding monitoring and verification technology
sections.summary: Asks whether the Government can fund remote sensing and emerging technologies to lower monitoring, reporting and verification costs for SMEs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Can the Government fund the installation of remote sensing and other emerging technologies that bring down the cost of monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV), which underpins the activity of carbon pricing, thus lowering the barrier to entry for these SMEs?

sections.label: Taxing imported goods' carbon content
sections.summary: Asks whether the Government can explore taxing the carbon content of imported goods to deter carbon leakage.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: To deter carbon leakage, can the Government also explore taxing the carbon content of imported goods?

sections.label: Carbon tax and electricity cost
sections.summary: States that raising the carbon tax to $25 per tonne will raise retail electricity cost within fluctuations seen since 2021.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Increasing the carbon tax to $25 per tonne will raise the retail cost of electricity by an amount well within the fluctuations we have been seeing since 2021.

sections.label: Decarbonisation business and job opportunity
sections.summary: States decarbonisation is a generation-defining business and job opportunity, and Singaporean companies are well-positioned to lead.

sentences.speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
sentences.text: Decarbonisation is a generation-defining business and job opportunity, and our Singaporean companies are well-positioned to lead the way.

sections.label: Carbon price increase proposal
sections.summary: The Bill proposes raising carbon pricing from $5 to $45 a tonne from 2026 to 2027, with a further rise to S$50-S$80 by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The Bill proposes an increase in carbon pricing from the current $5 a tonne to $45 a tonne from 2026 to 2027.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong also announced in Budget 2022 that it will be raised to between S$50 and S$80 by 2030.

sections.label: International carbon price benchmarks
sections.summary: The speaker cites international benchmarks proposing higher carbon prices by 2030 than Singapore's.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: I fully agree with the Deputy Prime Minister on his comments.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: But if we look at international benchmarks, the World Bank-supported High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices proposes US$50 to US$100 is needed by 2030, the OECD provides a central estimate of €120, while the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE)'s Grantham Institute suggests a price of US$145.

sections.label: International carbon credits offset limit
sections.summary: The Bill allows companies to offset up to 5% of taxable emissions via ICCs, but clause 33B lets the Minister permit excess surrendering.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The Government seems to acknowledge this by allowing companies to offset up to 5% of taxable emissions via ICCs in this Bill.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: However, clause 33B of the Bill currently provides an exception where the Minister may "permit eligible international carbon credits to be surrendered in excess of the prescribed limit in any particular case or class of cases".

sections.label: US Inflation Reduction Act climate funding
sections.summary: The US IRA directs over US$400 billion in climate and energy spending over 10 years, funded by drug pricing reform and a corporate minimum tax.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: The US appears to be leading the way with its recent IRA, which directs significant funding for climate efforts through a mix of tax incentives, grants and loan guarantees, and is set to be funded by prescription drug pricing reform and a 15% corporate minimum tax among others.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Over US$400 billion in spending over the next 10 years will be on climate and energy initiatives, but more importantly, the multiplier effect of this from both the public and private sector would mean significantly higher investments into a new growth area.

sections.label: Carbon budget and 2030 emissions target
sections.summary: The IPCC AR6 says the 1.5 degree carbon budget could be used up in under eight years, and the speaker questions the 2030 emissions target.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: Based on the IPCC's AR6, the global carbon budget to stay below the 1.5 degree celsius warming threshold could be used up in less than eight years from now.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
sentences.text: While the reduction in 2030 target emissions of 60 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent from 65 million tonnes is definitely welcomed, does it mean that we will still reach 65 million tonnes of CO2 or higher ahead of previous forecasts, even as we set a lower 2030 emissions target?

sections.label: Singapore carbon price increase signal
sections.summary: Singapore's carbon price increase from S$5 to $25, then $45, and a S$50-80 target by 2030 signals companies to mitigate emissions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The increase in carbon prices in Singapore – from S$5 per tonne of CO2, to the proposed $25 per tonne of CO2 from 2024 to 2025; and then to $45 per tonne of CO2 from 2026 to 2027, with a further step up to a target range of S$50 to 80 per tonne of CO2 by 2030 – sends a strong signal for large emitters as well as all other companies in Singapore at large to mitigate their emissions, at least, to be line with Singapore's carbon reduction goals.

sections.label: Singapore carbon pricing competitiveness risk
sections.summary: Singapore is the only Southeast Asian country with a carbon pricing regime, and its carbon price risks carbon leakage and impacts competitiveness.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: At this time, Singapore remains the only country in Southeast Asia with a carbon pricing regime in place and with our carbon price at levels being debated today, we will potentially face the risk of carbon leakage and Singapore's competitiveness will be impacted.

sections.label: Low-carbon electricity import plans
sections.summary: Current plans have Singapore importing four gigawatts of low-carbon electricity only by 2035.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Current plans have Singapore importing four gigawatts of low-carbon electricity only by 2035.

sections.label: EU carbon border adjustment mechanisms
sections.summary: Jurisdictions like the EU will introduce carbon border adjustment mechanisms in 2023, to be operational by 2026.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Jurisdictions like the EU will be introducing carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAM) in 2023 to be operational by 2026.

sections.label: Eligible ICCs for carbon tax
sections.summary: From 2024 onwards, companies may use eligible ICCs in lieu of paying carbon tax for up to 5% of taxable emissions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: From the Budget announcement, companies will have the option to use eligible ICCs in lieu of paying carbon tax for up to 5% of their taxable emissions from 2024 onwards.

sections.label: Questions on ICCs and carbon tax
sections.summary: The passage asks why the Government caps ICC use at 5% and what its carbon tax implementation plan is beyond large emitters.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: What are the reasons as to why the Government is not allowing for a higher than 5% of a company's taxable emissions to be paid for with qualified ICCs?

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: To further cascade the change of behaviours to one of a low-carbon economy, especially with Singapore's updated climate ambitions, what is the Government's implementation plan for carbon tax for companies beyond the large emitters?

sections.label: Support for Carbon Tax Amendment Bill
sections.summary: The speaker supports the Carbon Tax (Amendment) Bill notwithstanding the clarifications given.

sentences.speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, I support the Carbon Tax (Amendment) Bill.

sections.label: Carbon price increase and revenues
sections.summary: Carbon price is proposed to rise to $25 per tonne by 2024 and $45 by 2026, raising questions on revenue use and living costs.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: The carbon price is proposed to increase five times to $25 per tonne of emissions by 2024 and $45 by 2026.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: According to the World Bank's State and Trends of Carbon Pricing 2022, this would mean that Singapore would lead Asia in carbon prices.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: In addition, with the significant increases in carbon tax, I would like to ask the Minister what the plans are for these additional revenues.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I understand that there are programmes already in place to incentivise and support environmental sustainability.

sentences.speaker: Mr Mark Chay (Nominated Member)
sentences.text: I am also concerned about how the increase in carbon prices will impact the daily living costs in Singapore and what are the Government's plans to ensure that energy prices remain stable.

sections.label: Singapore carbon tax introduction
sections.summary: Singapore introduced the carbon tax in 2019 at a nominal $5 per tonne of CO2 emission to help society transit and adjust.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Singapore introduced the carbon tax in 2019 at a nominal $5 per tonne of CO2 emission to help the whole of our society transit and adjust.

sections.label: Cushioning carbon tax impact
sections.summary: The passage asks how to cushion the impact of carbon tax for which groups while maintaining the price signal and bringing society along.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: How do we cushion the impact – and for which groups – yet maintain the integrity of the price signal of carbon across the whole of society and bring all segments in our society along in this journey towards a low-carbon future?

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: It is heartening to hear the Government's commitment to use part of the carbon tax revenues to help Singaporeans cushion the impact, by way of, for example, more utilities rebates and public transport vouchers (PTVs), but can the Government share more of its thinking about how it plans to deploy this, for whom, how much and what would be its guiding principles and key considerations as it moves ahead in this direction?

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: Singapore was the first to introduce a carbon tax in the region.

sentences.speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
sentences.text: And in very short order, Singapore will have the highest carbon tax in the region.

sections.label: Carbon tax rates and emissions targets
sections.summary: The passage cites views that proposed carbon taxes are low, mentions green dividend and green fund, and states Singapore will peak at 60 million tonnes CO2 in 2030 and aim for net-zero by 2050.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: In terms of the carbon tax rates, I quoted a series of various numbers – by the World Bank, the OECD and various sources, and I think that is also consistent with what some of the feedback that was provided through the MSE consultations.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: There are views that based on the existing level of carbon taxes that we have proposed, it is actually on the low end of both the scientific recommendations as well as what is proposed by some of these other organisations in their studies.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: In particular, when it comes to supporting households, we have talked about, for example, reducing the impact of higher carbon taxes on households, such as via a green dividend and a green fund.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: These are mechanisms which can be potentially put in place on top of the various utilities rebates which the Government has also put forth.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Instead of peaking at 65 million tonnes CO2 in 2030, Singapore will step up our efforts to peak earlier and reduce carbon emissions to 60 million tonnes CO2 in 2030.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: And instead of just halving our long-term carbon emissions to 33 million tonnes CO2, we will aim for a stretched target of net-zero carbon in 2050.

sections.label: Progressive carbon tax implementation
sections.summary: The carbon tax will be implemented progressively, increasing from $5 per tonne CO2 emissions to $25 next year and $45 in 2026.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Also, the carbon tax will be implemented in a progressive manner.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: It will be increased from $5 per tonne CO2 emissions to $25 next year, and to $45 in 2026.

sections.label: Singapore emissions by sector
sections.summary: In Singapore, 40% of national carbon emissions come from the power sector and another 45% from industries.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: In Singapore, 40% of our national carbon emissions come from the power sector while another 45% is attributed to the industries.

sections.label: Carbon credits and ICC limit
sections.summary: Carbon credits offer a decarbonisation pathway for hard-to-abate sectors, but only up to 5% of emissions is eligible for ICC surrender.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Carbon credits provide a decarbonisation pathway for hard-to-abate sectors and represent an opportunity to support emissions reductions globally.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: However, under the ICC framework, only up to 5% of the carbon emissions is eligible for ICC surrender.

sections.label: Bloomberg carbon credit price forecast
sections.summary: Bloomberg analysis says tighter regulations may raise carbon credit prices 30 times by 2029 to $224 per tonne, tapering to $120 in 2050.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: According to the Bloomberg market analysis, under tighter regulations, carbon credit prices may rise 30 times by 2029 to $224 per tonne CO2 before tapering to $120 in 2050.

sections.label: Raising 5% carbon credit limit
sections.summary: Domestic demand is needed to jumpstart the carbon trading hub, so the Minister is asked to consider raising the 5% limit longer term.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: To jumpstart this carbon trading hub, there should also be substantial domestic demand for carbon credits.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Hence, I hope the Minister would consider increasing the limit beyond 5% of taxable emissions in the longer term.

sections.label: Funding National Hydrogen Strategy
sections.summary: Hydrogen solutions and technological breakthroughs are needed for long-term energy needs, so carbon tax revenue should partly fund the National Hydrogen Strategy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: To overcome the twin-wicked problems of climate crisis and energy crisis, we will have to leverage technological breakthroughs and succeed in delivering hydrogen solutions, in order to address our long-term energy needs.

sentences.speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
sentences.text: Hence, I hope that part of the revenue collected from carbon tax will be channelled to fund the National Hydrogen Strategy.

sections.label: Carbon tax pricing emissions
sections.summary: The carbon tax prices carbon to guide company investment decisions and spur emissions reductions while giving flexibility for economic sense.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: The carbon tax forms a key part of this effort.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: It prices carbon to guide investment decisions by companies and spurs company to reduce their emissions, while giving them the flexibility to do so in a way that makes the most economic sense.

sections.label: Carbon tax coverage of emissions
sections.summary: The carbon tax is targeted at key emissions nodes in the economy and will cover about 80% of total carbon emissions.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: In this way, the carbon tax is targeted to apply to the key nodes of emissions in our economy.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: It will cover about 80% of our total carbon emissions.

sections.label: Announced carbon tax rates
sections.summary: The Government announced changes to carbon tax rates ahead of time, spelling out rates up to 2027 and a range up to 2030.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: It is with these factors in mind that the Government decided to announce the changes to our carbon tax rates ahead of time.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: We have spelt out the rates for up to 2027 and provided a range for up to 2030.

sections.label: Transition framework for companies
sections.summary: A transition framework will give eligible companies transitory allowances for a portion of their emissions while supporting decarbonisation and Singapore's competitive edge.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: The sustainability journey is one that we walk together – and we seek to smoothen the transition path for companies – by providing the necessary support for their decarbonisation while maintaining Singapore's competitive edge.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: Hence, we will introduce a transition framework which will provide eligible companies with transitory allowances for a portion of their emissions.

sections.label: Allowances cover portion of emissions
sections.summary: The transition allowances will only cover a portion of companies' emissions and will not run counter to long-term goals.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: We are mindful that the transition allowances provided will not run counter to our long-term goals.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: I want to ensure and emphasise that the amount of allowances provided will only be for a portion of the companies' emissions.

sections.label: Allowances for carbon tax only
sections.summary: The allowances are provided only for the carbon tax and are not tradable.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: To address Mr Don Wee's query, the allowances are only provided for the carbon tax and are not tradable.

sections.label: Existing investments and commitments eligible
sections.summary: Only existing investments and commitments will be eligible for transitory allowances.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: Furthermore, only existing investments and commitments will be eligible for transitory allowances.

sections.label: Mitigating carbon leakage risk
sections.summary: The transition framework helps mitigate carbon leakage risk so companies avoid shifting operations to jurisdictions with lower or no effective carbon prices.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: The transition framework will also help to mitigate the risk of carbon leakage – a risk that many Members spoke about in their speeches – so that we avoid companies shifting operations to other jurisdictions with lower or no effective carbon prices.

sections.label: No CBAM plans
sections.summary: Singapore has no plans to introduce a CBAM, as tariff barriers would disadvantage its companies and have limited impact on carbon leakage.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: A CBAM proposes a carbon tariff on carbon-intensive imports to stem carbon leakage to countries without a carbon price.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: We currently have no plans to introduce a CBAM because as a small market, putting in place tariff barriers would disadvantage our own companies and have a limited impact on stemming carbon leakage.

sections.label: Company energy efficiency schemes
sections.summary: Schemes like REG(E) and E2F help companies and SMEs improve energy efficiency, reducing energy costs and carbon tax impact.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: For instance, we have schemes to help our companies like our SMEs improve their energy efficiency, which will, in turn, reduce their energy costs as well as the impact of the carbon tax.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: These include the Resource Efficiency Grant for Emissions (REG(E)) administered by EDB as well as the Energy Efficiency Fund (E2F) administered by NEA.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: One project under the REG(E) scheme supported the replacement of a facility's existing chiller system with a more energy-efficient one, achieving energy savings of more than 3,600MWh.

sections.label: E2F grant cap raised
sections.summary: The E2F was enhanced in April, raising the grant support cap for energy-efficient technologies from 50% to 70% of qualifying costs.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: For example, the E2F was just enhanced about six months ago in April this year.

sentences.speaker: The Minister of State for Trade and Industry (Ms Low Yen Ling)
sentences.text: We raised the grant support cap for the adoption of energy-efficient technologies, from what used to be 50%, we raised it to 70% of the qualifying costs.

sections.label: Revised carbon tax incentives
sections.summary: Revised carbon tax levels will incentivise energy and carbon efficiency and favour additional decarbonisation solutions like CCUS and low-carbon hydrogen.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: The revised carbon tax levels will incentivise energy and carbon efficiency in all sectors and tilt the scales in favour of additional decarbonisation solutions, such as CCUS and low-carbon hydrogen.

sections.label: ICC framework criteria
sections.summary: The ICC framework will be underpinned by robust criteria, minimally aligned to internationally endorsed CORSIA standards.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Our ICC framework will be underpinned by a set of robust criteria, which will, minimally, be aligned to the CORSIA standards which have been endorsed internationally.

sections.label: ICC whitelist publication
sections.summary: Standards must be mutually agreed with partner countries, and a whitelist of acceptable ICCs will be published.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: These are standards which must be mutually agreed upon when we conclude carbon credits collaboration with partner countries.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: We will publish a whitelist of ICCs that are acceptable, which will highlight the eligible host countries, carbon crediting programmes and methodologies.

sections.label: International Carbon Credits Registry tender
sections.summary: NEA will call a tender this week to develop the International Carbon Credits Registry.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: On the carbon credits registry, later this week, NEA will be calling a tender for the development of the International Carbon Credits Registry, or ICC Registry.

sections.label: NEA MOUs with carbon programmes
sections.summary: NEA signed MOUs with Verra and Gold Standard, letting companies buy eligible credits to offset carbon tax liabilities.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: In July, NEA signed MOUs with leading carbon crediting programmes, namely, Verra and Gold Standard, which, together, account for over 70% of global carbon credit issuances.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: With these MOUs in place, companies will be able to acquire eligible ICC from projects registered with these programmes and surrender them to offset part of their carbon tax liabilities.

sections.label: Five percent facility-level limit
sections.summary: The facility-level limit starts at 5% to prioritise domestic abatement efforts.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: As mentioned earlier, we are starting with 5% as the facility-level limit to prioritise domestic abatement efforts.

sections.label: Reviewing facility-level limit over time
sections.summary: The facility-level limit will be reviewed over time and aligned with international best practices as carbon markets develop.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: If we start putting too many rules, it may make the scheme ineffective even if it can be the most transparent in the world.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: We will review the facility-level limit over time and align with international best practices, as carbon markets develop.

sections.label: Carbon tax threshold coverage
sections.summary: The 25,000 tonne carbon tax threshold applies the carbon price efficiently and covers around 80% of Singapore's emissions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: The current carbon tax threshold of 25,000 tonnes ensures that the carbon price is efficiently applied at key nodes of the economy and maximises coverage while it minimises – I would say optimises – the administrative burden on businesses.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: This covers around 80% of Singapore's emissions, one of the most comprehensive in the world.

sections.label: Reportable facilities small emissions share
sections.summary: Reportable facilities contribute only about 1% of Singapore's emissions, adding little to the 80% coverage.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Furthermore, as reportable facilities contribute only about 1% of Singapore's emissions, it would add little to the already high coverage of 80%.

sections.label: Carbon tax level range comparison
sections.summary: A quoted range of $80 to $133 is significantly higher than the stated $50 to $80 carbon tax level.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: He quoted, if I am not wrong, $80 to $133 as a range and with $100 as a useful midpoint or benchmark for our carbon tax level.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: So, this $80 to $133 is significantly higher than what we have stated, which is $50 to $80.

sections.label: Carbon tax timing and 2030
sections.summary: A suggestion to push back the tax is met with a proposal to raise the carbon tax in 2024, leaving six years to 2030.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Also, he has suggested that maybe we should push back the tax.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: We are suggesting that we raise the carbon tax in 2024 and that leaves us six years to 2030.

sections.label: Next carbon tax step
sections.summary: The next step is $25 per tonne, rising from $5 to $25 in 2024.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Just for Members' information, $25 per tonne, is really our next step – from $5 to $25 in 2024.

sections.label: Utilities bill impact for HDB
sections.summary: At $25 per tonne, the carbon tax rise would increase the utilities bill by about $4 per month for an average 4-room HDB household.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: At $25 per tonne, the rise in carbon tax would translate to an estimated increase of about $4 per month in the utilities bill for an average 4-room Housing and Development Board (HDB) household.

sections.label: U-Save rebates and inflation
sections.summary: Other inflationary pressures come from other factors, and the U-Save rebates for households cost the Government $580 million for FY2022.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Other effects, other inflationary pressures are coming in because of other factors.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: And just the utilities bills support, the U-Save rebates that I mentioned that go to households, cost the Government $580 million for FY2022.

sections.label: Economy and carbon tax transition
sections.summary: The announced carbon tax levels will be stuck with while taking suggestions into consideration, keeping an eye on economic competitiveness during the transition to a low-carbon economy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: But we have to take into consideration the next point, which is really the economy.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: We have announced the carbon tax and we have repeatedly been telling companies that these are the levels that are going to come.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: We will stick with these, but we will take your suggestions into consideration.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: And as we make the transition to a low-carbon economy, we must keep an eye on our economic competitiveness, so that Singapore remains an attractive investment and business destination and generates green growth opportunities and good jobs for Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: The proposed changes, as set out in this Bill, have been carefully considered in close consultation with the industry and the public.

sections.label: Limiting allowances in perpetuity
sections.summary: A member asks whether the Government would support a legislative mechanism limiting allowances over time to prevent a company receiving maximum allowances in perpetuity.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Nevertheless, having a more ambitious aggregate target may still allow either this Government or some future Government, in theory, in principle, to prop up a company with a fairly generous level of allowances in perpetuity, for a long time, and to do so in a manner that is not transparent.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: If I am a company that is a large emitter, I would want to know that there is a certain amount of transparency about which entities are being given allowances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: So, I would like to pose this clarification, which is that, is the Government open to having some kind of legislative mechanism that would limit the allowances, in terms of time, to prevent this possibility of a company in perpetuity getting allowances up to the maximum that is referred to in the point of reference.

sections.label: Public registry of allowance recipients
sections.summary: A member asks whether the Government would consider a public registry showing which entities receive allowances, without disclosing allowance or ICC amounts.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: I want to stress again that we are not calling for the amounts of allowances to be disclosed or the amounts of ICCs being used to be disclosed.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: But I would like to ask again whether the Government would consider that a public registry may actually strengthen confidence in the regime buy-in to a new carbon price hike, which does impose significant burdens on companies and on households, and would impose a certain amount of public accountability, for the public to know that these are the entities that are getting allowances and we are able to see that these entities are doing their best or they are contributing back to the country, they are making progress towards lowering their emissions and so on.

sections.label: Publishing aggregate allowance figures
sections.summary: A member asks whether the Government would publish, in aggregate, the number of allowances awarded and the emissions covered by allowances.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Would the Government be open to publishing the number of allowances that have been awarded, just in aggregate, and the extent of emissions that are covered by allowances in aggregate, in the future, if they do not want this public registry proposal?

sections.label: Updated 2030 NDC commitment
sections.summary: The Singapore Government has just updated its 2030 NDC commitment.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: The Singapore Government just updated our 2030 NDC commitment.

sections.label: Allowances cover only portion of emissions
sections.summary: The allowance covers only a portion of emissions and is based on internationally recognised efficiency standards and facilities' decarbonisation plans.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: I want to assure him that even as we avail the allowance, it is really only for a portion of the emissions.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: It is given based on internationally recognised efficiency standards, where available, as well as the individual facilities' decarbonisation plans.

sections.label: EITE companies' investment and employment
sections.summary: EITE companies have invested billions in Singapore, contributing about S$21 billion in value-add and employing about 29,000 workers.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: We talked about some of these sectors and Ms Janet Ang reminded us that the EITE companies have poured in significant, in fact, billions of dollars of investment in Singapore over the decades, creating very good jobs for Singaporeans.

sentences.speaker: Ms Low Yen Ling
sentences.text: These EITE companies are key investors and are global leaders that collectively contribute about S$21 billion in value-add and employ about 29,000 workers here in Singapore.

sections.label: Confidentiality for public officers engaging companies
sections.summary: Public officers should engage companies confidently while keeping commercial confidentiality, so individual disclosure will be kept confidential.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: What we want is to make sure that our public officers have the ability to engage companies confidently, keeping in mind their obligation to maintain commercial confidentiality for the simple reasons that the companies may be competitors themselves.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: So, like many of these discussions, like many of these plans, we want to respect each other's requirements, so we have taken the stand that we will keep individual disclosure confidential.

sections.label: Range of $50 to $80
sections.summary: The stated range is $50 to $80.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Oh, we have – $50 to $80 is our range.

sections.label: Comparing two pay ranges
sections.summary: One range is $50 to $80, while the other range is $58 to $133.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Our range is $50 to $80; your range is $58 to $133.

sections.label: Target rate for 2024
sections.summary: A question asks whether the target rate for 2024 will be stated, offering to go with the Government's proposed number.

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: Are you going to say what is your target rate for 2024?

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: We can go with the Government's proposed number.

sections.label: Comfortable with original $25
sections.summary: They are not opposed to the original path and are comfortable with the original $25 for the next year and the subsequent year.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: Again, we are not opposed to the original path.

sentences.speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
sentences.text: So, for the next year and the subsequent year, we are comfortable with going with that $25 that was originally there.

sections.label: Confidentiality provisions and Fourth Schedule
sections.summary: A question asks if the Minister means specific legal provisions would be breached, noting the Fourth Schedule of the CPA restricts disclosure to specified public officers.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
sentences.text: Is the Minister saying that the confidentiality provisions that will be breached are specific legal provisions that would be breached?

sentences.speaker: Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien
sentences.text: I believe the Fourth Schedule of the CPA restricts disclosure to specified public officers.

sections.label: President's recommendation not forthcoming
sections.summary: Amendments in Mr Leon Perera's name cannot be moved because the President's recommendation is not forthcoming, and he asks when concurrence was sought.

sentences.speaker: The Chairman
sentences.text: As the President’s recommendation is not forthcoming for amendments (1) to (3) and (8) to (12) standing in Mr Leon Perera's name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement, these amendments cannot be moved.

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Mr Chairman, Sir, on a point of order, may I pose some questions to the hon Minister, the Leader of the House, on the process surrounding how the President was approached and how the recommendation was sought?

sentences.speaker: Mr Leon Perera
sentences.text: Specifically, what I would like to ask is when was the concurrence of the President sought for my amendments?

sections.label: Article 59(2) President's recommendation
sections.summary: Article 59(2) of the Constitution requires the President's recommendation for a Bill or amendment making provision for stated financial matters.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: Article 59(2) of the Constitution provides that the recommendation of the President is required for a Bill or an amendment that makes provision, whether directly or indirectly, for one of the stated financial matters.

sections.label: Less than 48 hours notice
sections.summary: The speaker says less than 48 hours' notice was given with no follow-up by the Workers' Party, and the President's recommendation is not given.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: I must say I do find that when you give the Government less than 48 hours' notice, and not to mention the fact that there was no follow-up on the part of the Workers' Party even to find out whether anything would be done in this respect, I have to say that I find that it was somewhat — let us put it this way: you gave less than 48 hours and somebody had to do the running for you.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: But in any event, the President's recommendation is not given for the Member's amendments.

sections.label: Amendments not put to President
sections.summary: The amendments were not put forward to the President, which is in order as the requirement safeguards the Government's financial initiative.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: And as the amendments could not be supported, they were not put forward to the President for the President's recommendation.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: This is perfectly in order as the Constitutional requirement, for the President's recommendation to be sought for amendments with financial implications, is a procedure that safeguards the Government's financial initiative.

sentences.speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
sentences.text: The President would act in accordance with the Government's advice in giving, or not giving, the required recommendation.

sections.label: Register contents and Minister's reason
sections.summary: The register shall contain information on the registered person, the emissions year of permitted excess, and the Minister's reason for lifting the limit.

sentences.speaker: Ms He Ting Ru
sentences.text: The register shall contain information that includes information relating to the registered person, the emissions year where the registered person was permitted to exceed the prescribed limit for international carbon credit usage, and the Minister's reason for deciding to lift the prescribed limit.".
